entries.heading: 7.4 SLE and the exponent set
entries.text: Definition 7.3 (chordal SLE ). Let B t be a standard Brownian motion and t= \,B t. The Loewner flow in the upper half-plane is the solution of and the SLE trace is (t)=g t^{-1}( t). Theorem 7.4 (Lawler–Schramm–Werner 2001). The scaling limit of the critical percolation interface on the triangular lattice is SLE 6. The parameter is fixed by the locality property: among all SLE , only =6 has a law invariant under restricting the domain, up to time reparametrisation. (The restriction property is a different condition, associated with =8/3.) Locality is exactly the continuum version of the domain Markov property combined with colour symmetry, which percolation possesses at p=1/2. From =6 the exponents follow by computing Brownian intersection exponents. The result is Consistency check. With these values, All four relations close exactly, which is a strong indication that no digit is wrong. The one-arm exponent is / =5/48: A reported exponent of n^{-2/3} is not consistent with this value, and the discrepancy is easy to detect because / must equal 5/48 for the exponent set to be self-consistent. Chapter 14 records the correction history.

entries.heading: 7.5 What the two-dimensional solution does and does not give
entries.text: It gives the exponents, the crossing probabilities, the arm exponents, and the conformal invariance of the scaling limit — for the triangular lattice, and for lattices connected to it by star–triangle transformations. It gives, in principle, the full continuum description of the critical geometry. It does not give the threshold on an arbitrary lattice. Cardy's formula is about the critical point; it says nothing about where the critical point is. The threshold remains a lattice-dependent quantity, known exactly for a handful of lattices (Chapter 4) and numerically for the rest. It also does not give the full scaling limit of the cluster as a set, only of the interfaces. The collection of all interfaces — the "full scaling limit" — is described by the Brownian loop soup / CLE technology, which is a substantial theory in its own right. For the purposes of this atlas, the interface statement is enough: every exponent in the table follows from it, and every numerical check of two-dimensional percolation can be phrased as a check of the Cardy formula or of an arm exponent.

entries.heading: 7.6 Numerical fingerprints
entries.text: Three numbers identify critical two-dimensional percolation beyond reasonable doubt: 1. the crossing probability at p c equals 1/2 at aspect ratio 1 (and follows Cardy's curve for other aspect ratios); 2. the one-arm probability decays as n^{-5/48}; 3. the cluster-size distribution decays as n^{-1-1/ }=n^{-96/91}=n^{-1.0549 }. A simulation that reproduces (1) but not (2) has a finite-size problem; one that reproduces (2) but not (3) has a cluster-counting problem. The three together are a much stronger check than any single exponent fit, and the benchmark suite in this repository reports all three.

entries.chapterTitle: High dimensions and the lace expansion
entries.heading: High dimensions and the lace expansion
entries.text: Above six dimensions, percolation forgets its lattice. The exponents take their mean-field values, the order parameter is smooth at p c, and the whole theory reduces to a branching process with corrections that can be bounded. The tool that proves this is the lace expansion, one of the few non-perturbative methods in critical phenomena. This chapter explains what the expansion is, why its convergence threshold is d 11 rather than d 6, and why the gap matters.

entries.chapterTitle: High dimensions and the lace expansion
entries.heading: 8.1 Mean-field from the Bethe lattice, done correctly
entries.text: The Bethe lattice (Cayley tree) of degree z is the d limit: no loops, so connectivity is a branching process. It is the one model where everything is exact. Bond percolation. Each edge is open with probability p. Let r be the probability that a given vertex, reached along an open edge, is connected to infinity through its descendants. The vertex has z-1 descendant edges, each open with probability p and leading to a subtree that percolates with probability r, independently. Hence and the root is connected to infinity iff at least one of its z edges is open and leads to a percolating subtree: The trivial solution r=0 is always present. A nonzero solution appears when the right-hand side has slope exceeding 1 at r=0: So p c=1/(z-1). For site percolation the recursion for an occupied vertex is r=1-(1-pr)^{z-1} and the root probability is =p[1-(1-pr)^z]; the extra factor p cancels at the threshold, so p c=1/(z-1) again. Exponents. Put p=p c(1+ ) with 0 small. Expanding the recursion to second order, so zp cr and =1. The mean cluster size is the expected progeny of a Galton–Watson process with mean p(z-1): so =1. At criticality the offspring distribution has mean one and finite variance, so the cluster size is in the domain of attraction of a stable law with {P}( C 0 =n) n^{-3/2}, which gives 1+1/ =3/2, i.e. =2. Finally, the relation = (d-2+ )/2 at the upper critical dimension d=6 with =0 gives 1= 2, so =1/2; the correlation length behaves as (p c-p)^{-1/2}, which can also be checked directly from the recursion. The fractal dimension is d f=d- / =6-2=4. Why the Bethe lattice is not a lattice. It has no cycles, so it is not a subgraph of {Z}^d for any finite d. Its exponents coincide with the mean-field values because the branching approximation becomes exact when loops are negligible, and loops are negligible above d c. The coincidence is a theorem above six dimensions, not an analogy.

entries.chapterTitle: High dimensions and the lace expansion
entries.heading: 8.2 The triangle condition
entries.text: Write p for the two-point function. The triangle condition is (Aizenman–Newman 1984; Barsky–Aizenman 1987 introduced it for percolation.) The name comes from the diagram: three propagators joining two vertices, i.e. a triangle in the dual representation, or a theta graph in the direct representation. Theorem 8.1 (Aizenman–Newman; Barsky–Aizenman). If the triangle condition holds at p c, then the mean-field exponents hold: = =1, =1/2, =2, =0, d f=4, and is twice differentiable at p c with '(p c) 0. The proof is a combination of the infrared bound (a Fourier-space inequality for ) with a differential inequality for ; it does not require the lace expansion. The triangle condition itself is what needs to be verified, and that is where the lace expansion enters. Why the condition is d 6. Suppose the mean-field form (x) x ^{-(d-2)} holds. Then (k) k ^{-2} and which is finite exactly when d 6. At d=6 the integral diverges logarithmically; the divergence is the source of the logarithmic corrections to mean-field behaviour at the upper critical dimension. The real-space version of the same count: the theta graph consists of three paths, each of scaling dimension d-2, joining two branch points. It is finite when 3(d-2) 2d, i.e. d 6. For a self-avoiding walk the corresponding diagram has two paths and one loop, 2(d-2) d, giving the familiar d c=4. The extra propagator is why percolation's upper critical dimension is two higher than the walk's.

entries.chapterTitle: High dimensions and the lace expansion
entries.heading: 8.3 The lace expansion
entries.text: The lace expansion rewrites (x) as a sum over "laced" graphs — trees decorated with overlaps — and shows that the series converges when d is large. The first term is the tree (mean-field) contribution; each additional lace costs a factor of order 1/d. Theorem 8.2 (Hara–Slade 1990; Fitzner–van der Hofstad 2017). For nearest-neighbour bond percolation on {Z}^d with d 11, the triangle condition holds at p c and the mean-field exponents obtain. Moreover The history of the threshold is instructive. Hara and Slade proved the result for d 19 in 1990; Fitzner and van der Hofstad (2017) brought the threshold down to d 11. Each improvement required a sharper estimate on the lace expansion's remainder, not a new idea. The gap between d 6 (where the triangle condition should hold) and d 11 (where it is proved) remains open; closing it needs estimates that the current expansion does not supply. What the expansion does not do. It gives no information about p c itself beyond its existence; it is a statement about exponents and about the smoothness of . And it gives nothing at d=6, where the logarithmic corrections require a separate analysis (Hara–Slade's work at the upper critical dimension, and later refinements).

entries.chapterTitle: High dimensions and the lace expansion
entries.heading: 8.4 The three-dimensional problem
entries.text: Three dimensions is where the theory is least complete and most needed: materials, porous media, biological tissues are three-dimensional. The numerical values are excellent and the rigorous values are absent. The best current estimates come from large-scale Monte Carlo with finite-size scaling: from Wang, Zhou, Zhang, Garoni and Deng (2013), with L up to 512 and about 2.5 10^7 samples per size. Converting, =0.8764(1), =0.4181(1), = (2- )=1.793(3), =-0.046(2), =5.29(1), d f=2.5229(1). The internal consistency of these numbers (Chapter 6, Section 6.2) is impressive, and independent methods agree. But consistency is not proof: the exponents could in principle be the limit of a sequence of effective exponents that has not converged. No one believes this, but the belief is supported by the agreement of many methods rather than by a theorem.

entries.chapterTitle: High dimensions and the lace expansion
entries.heading: 8.5 The geometry above six dimensions
entries.text: The statement d f=4 at d 6 is strange at first: the cluster is a four-dimensional object living in a higher-dimensional space, so it is extremely sparse. Its structure has two parts: a backbone that carries the cycles and the current, and dangling ends attached to it. The dangling ends carry much of the mass but no current. This is why the conductivity exponent t and the mass exponent d f are different quantities, and why the "anomalous" conductivity of percolation networks is not a small correction but a distinct phenomenon (Chapter 12). The same two-scale picture explains the paradox that =1/2 and d f=4 coexist: the correlation length grows as ^{-1/2}, the mass at that scale as ^4= ^{-2}, and the percolation probability as ^{-2}= , which is =1. Nothing is inconsistent; the cluster simply has two independent length scales once d 6.

entries.heading: The random-cluster model
entries.text: The random-cluster (RC) model is percolation with a reward for forming clusters. It is the Fortuin–Kasteleyn representation of the q-state Potts model, and at q=1 it is ordinary percolation. Its value in this atlas is twofold: it gives a rigorous bridge between percolation and spin systems, and it supplies the algorithms (Swendsen–Wang, Edwards–Sokal) that made cluster updates standard in computational physics.

entries.heading: 9.1 Definition
entries.text: Let G=(V,E) be finite. For p [0,1] and q 0, put where k( ) is the number of connected components of the open subgraph, counting isolated vertices. At q=1 the cluster weight disappears and {p,1} is Bernoulli percolation. The parameter q need not be an integer for the measure to make sense, but the spin interpretation requires q \{2,3, \}.

entries.heading: 9.2 The Potts correspondence
entries.text: Proposition 9.1 (★). For integer q 2 and 0, the q-state Potts partition function equals Z G(p,q) up to an explicit factor, with p=1-e^{- }. Proof. For a single edge, the identity is a two-case check. Multiplying over edges and expanding the product, Summing over , the product of deltas forces to be constant on each connected component of (V, ), and each component can take any of q colours. There are q^{k( )} colourings, so using e^ -1=p/(1-p). The last factor is independent of and cancels in the normalisation. At q=2 this is the Ising model in its Fortuin–Kasteleyn form, and the percolation probability becomes the magnetisation: 0 is an increasing function of the probability that the origin is connected to the boundary. The correspondence is exact, not an analogy, and it is the reason percolation exponents can be computed from spin-model technology and vice versa.

entries.heading: 9.3 Consequences
entries.text: Shared critical points. The RC model has a phase transition at a value p c(q) that is the image of the Potts critical temperature. For q=2 on {Z}^2, the self-dual point is p c= 2/(1+ 2)=0.585786 , which corresponds to the Ising critical point (2 c)=1 under p=1-e^{-2 c}. The equality is a theorem, and it gives the Ising critical temperature on {Z}^2 without a transfer-matrix calculation. The value p=1/2 is the q=1 (percolation) special case, not the Ising point. Monotonicity in q. The RC measure is positively associated for q 1 and satisfies FKG; the percolation probability is monotone in p and, for fixed p, monotone in q in a suitable coupling. This is why increasing q can turn a continuous transition into a first-order one: the cluster reward favours a dense phase. Duality. On a planar graph the RC model has a dual model with transformed parameters; on the square lattice the self-dual curve is p= q/(1+ q), and at q=1 it reduces to p 1-p. The duality relations are the RC generalisation of Lemma 4.2 and are the cleanest route to the q-dependent critical points on the square and triangular lattices.

entries.heading: 9.4 Algorithms
entries.text: The RC representation is behind two of the most useful algorithms in Monte Carlo physics. Swendsen–Wang (1987). Given a spin configuration, form the Fortuin–Kasteleyn clusters by opening each edge with probability p=1-e^{-J} when the two endpoint spins agree and never otherwise, where J is the Potts coupling (for the Ising normalisation above, J=2 ). Then assign a fresh random colour to each cluster. The resulting spin configuration is stationary for the Potts measure. The update is non-local: it can flip an entire correlated region in one step, which is why it beats single-spin Metropolis near a critical point. Edwards–Sokal (1988). A joint update of spins and bonds that is a Gibbs sampler for the RC measure; it gives a systematic way to interpolate between the spin and cluster pictures and is the standard tool for measuring cluster observables. Neither algorithm changes the physics; both change the correlation time. At a critical point the single-spin Metropolis algorithm suffers critical slowing down with dynamic exponent z 2, while cluster algorithms reduce z substantially for Potts models. For percolation itself (q=1) the relevant algorithm is not Swendsen–Wang but the Newman–Ziff sweep of Chapter 11, which samples the whole coupling curve from one random edge order rather than from a Markov chain.

entries.heading: 9.5 What the RC model does not solve
entries.text: The RC model does not give the percolation threshold on a general lattice, because the q=1 model has no spin representation to solve. It does not give the full scaling limit in two dimensions except through the Coulomb-gas/SLE machinery, which is a separate development. And it does not make the three-dimensional exponents rigorous: the RC model at q=1 in d=3 is exactly as hard as percolation. What it does give is a language. Statements about percolation that are awkward in the Bernoulli picture — boundary conditions, wired/free limits, cluster weights, the meaning of "conditioning on a connection" — become natural in the RC picture. Much of the rigorous technology in this atlas (FKG, the matching theorem, the sharpness proofs) can be phrased in the RC language and then specialised to q=1.

entries.heading: Networks: degrees, cores, and coupling
entries.text: On a lattice every vertex has the same number of neighbours. On a network it does not, and the degree distribution becomes a control parameter as important as p. Three results carry most of the theory: the Molloy–Reed criterion for the existence of a giant component, the first-order character of k-core percolation, and the 2.4554 threshold of two fully coupled Erdős–Rényi networks. The last one is derived here from scratch, because it is easy to get the coupled-network recursion subtly wrong.

entries.heading: 10.1 The configuration model and the branching approximation
entries.text: Fix a degree sequence (k 1, ,k N) with k i=2M. The configuration model pairs the 2M stubs uniformly at random. In the limit N with a fixed degree distribution p k, the neighbourhood of a random vertex converges locally to a branching process: a vertex of degree k has k neighbours, and a neighbour reached along an edge has k-1 further edges, with the size-biased degree distribution The size bias is the only non-obvious ingredient. Choose a random edge and then a random endpoint: a vertex of degree k is chosen with probability proportional to k, not to p k. Getting this wrong is a common error in applied network papers.

entries.heading: 10.2 Molloy–Reed, with the calculation
entries.text: Retain each vertex independently with probability p (site dilution). Define as the probability that connectivity continues forever from a vertex reached along an edge. A retained neighbour of degree k continues if at least one of its k-1 other edges leads to a retained vertex that continues, so The giant component exists iff this equation has a positive solution, which happens iff the derivative at =0 exceeds one: Hence At full occupancy (p=1) this reduces to 2, the Molloy–Reed criterion. Under dilution the criterion is p( -1) 1, or equivalently p 1/( -1); 2 alone is not enough. The parameter is the branching factor of the size-biased walk; it is not the mean degree, and the two coincide only for Poisson degrees. The dilute fraction is f=1-p, so the critical removal fraction is For Erdős–Rényi degrees, k^2 = k ( k +1) and =c+1, giving f c=1-1/c, the familiar result that a random graph with mean degree c fragments when a fraction 1-1/c of vertices is removed. A common slip. It is tempting to write f c=1-1/ and to quote, in the same display, the correct expression 1- k /( k^2 - k ). The two are not equal: 1/ = k / k^2 , whereas the correct denominator is k^2 - k . The Erdős–Rényi special case is forgiving, which is why the error survives casual checks. The general formula is f c=1-1/( -1), and the difference matters for heavy-tailed degrees, where -1 and can differ by a large factor.

entries.heading: 10.3 Scale-free degrees: the disappearance of the threshold
entries.text: Take p k k^{- { {deg}}} for k m (the subscript distinguishes the degree exponent from the susceptibility exponent ). Then converges iff { {deg}} 3. Three regimes follow: - { {deg}} 3: =( { {deg}}-2)m/( { {deg}}-3) is finite, so f c=1-1/( -1) is a genuine threshold below one. - 2< { {deg}} 3: k^2 = , so = , f c=1: random removal never destroys the giant component in the infinite-size limit. - { {deg}} 2: even k diverges and the distribution needs a finite-N regularisation; the notion of a random graph with such degrees is delicate. The same network is extremely fragile under targeted removal: deleting vertices in decreasing degree order can destroy the giant component while most vertices remain. This is the "robust yet fragile" duality of Cohen, Erez, ben-Avraham and Havlin (2000) and Albert, Jeong and Barabási (2000). It is not a paradox: random removal samples the degree distribution proportionally, so the many low-degree vertices dominate; targeted removal hits the hubs that hold the network together.

entries.heading: 10.4 $k$-core percolation
entries.text: The k-core of a graph is obtained by repeatedly deleting vertices of current degree less than k. Unlike connectivity, the k-core requires local redundancy: a vertex survives if at least k of its neighbours survive. On an Erdős–Rényi graph with mean degree c, the 3-core appears discontinuously. Above a threshold c 3 3.35 (for the appearance of a non-empty 3-core in the undiluted graph; Dorogovtsev, Goltsev and Mendes 2006) the core is macroscopic; below it there is nothing. Under dilution the transition is also discontinuous, with a hysteresis loop if the process is run in reverse. The mechanism is a bootstrap-percolation feedback: losing one vertex can push several neighbours below the threshold, which removes more vertices, and the cascade either stops early or runs to completion. This is the cleanest example of a percolation transition whose type is changed by the local rule rather than by correlations. It matters in applications because "gradual degradation" is exactly what a k-core requirement removes: a system with a redundancy requirement fails abruptly, not gracefully.

entries.heading: 10.5 Two coupled networks and the constant 2.4554
entries.text: Model (Buldyrev et al. 2010). Two networks A and B on the same vertex set, with a one-to-one coupling. A vertex survives a round iff it is initially retained, belongs to the giant component of the surviving subgraph of A, and its partner belongs to the giant component of the surviving subgraph of B. Remove a fraction 1-p initially, apply the round repeatedly, and stop at the fixed point. After labelling partners by the same index, the one-to-one partner map is the identity, so the round is the intersection of the two giant components; pruning A and B in isolation is not the same algorithm and keeps vertices whose partner has already failed. Mean-field solution for Erdős–Rényi layers. Let be the fraction of vertices in the mutual giant component. A retained vertex is in it iff it has at least one neighbour in A that is in the mutual component, and the same in B. For Poisson degrees with mean c, the probability that none of the c neighbours qualifies is e^{-c }, and the two layers are independent given the vertex, so The trivial solution =0 always exists. A nontrivial solution appears when the right-hand side is tangent to the diagonal. Write t=c and f(t)=p(1-e^{-t})^2. Tangency requires The second gives 1/c=2p(1-e^{-t})e^{-t}. Dividing the first equation by the second, so e^{t}=1+2t. The nonzero root is t^ =1.256431 , giving For comparison, a single Erdős–Rényi layer has p c=1/c. Coupling therefore raises the threshold by a factor 2.4554, and the transition is first order : at p c the mutual component jumps from zero to a finite size ^ =t^ /c, because the nontrivial branch is born by a saddle-node bifurcation, not by a continuous bifurcation from zero. Two consequences are worth stating because they are often missed. First, the constant is not universal: it depends on the degree distribution and on the coupling pattern (one-to-one, partial, multiple). For a fully coupled pair of Poisson layers it is exactly the root of the transcendental equation above; for other degree distributions the same calculation gives a different number. Second, the first-order character is what makes the system dangerous: there is no early warning in the order parameter, and the cascade proceeds at a finite fraction of the network per step. Partial coupling. If only a fraction q of vertices are coupled, the recursion becomes a pair of equations for the two layers. For small coupling strength the transition returns to second order (Parshani, Buldyrev and Havlin 2010). The design lesson — prefer several weak couplings to one strong one — is the engineering content of the theory.

entries.heading: 10.6 Higher-order percolation
entries.text: On a simplicial complex or hypergraph, "connected" can mean k-th order connectivity (two k-simplices joined through a shared (k-1)-face), connectivity defined through Betti numbers, or connectivity defined through the Euler characteristic. Numerically, these definitions produce transitions that can be more continuous than the graph case, with a critical interval in which Betti numbers stay nonzero. There is no unified rigorous theory; the topic is in Chapter 13's list of open problems, and the numerics are sensitive to the definition used.

entries.heading: 10.7 Design rules that follow
entries.text: Four rules follow from this chapter and are used in Chapter 12's case studies. 1. Homogenise degrees to resist targeted attack; heterogenise to resist random failure. The two objectives conflict, and the conflict is quantified by f c=1-1/( -1) versus the targeted threshold. 2. Avoid single-point dependencies. One-to-one coupling turns a continuous transition into a first-order one; multiple coupling restores the continuous character. 3. Treat redundancy requirements as discontinuous. A k-core requirement removes the gradual regime; design the safety margin for the jump, not for the average. 4. Measure , not the mean degree. The mean degree is the wrong summary statistic for robustness; a network with the same mean degree and a heavier tail has a very different f c.

entries.chapterTitle: Measuring a threshold without fooling yourself
entries.heading: Measuring a threshold without fooling yourself
entries.text: A threshold is not a number that can be read off a single curve. Every finite sample has a rounded transition, and the rounding is not noise around a fixed answer: it is the answer changing with the system size. This chapter sets out a measurement protocol that separates the two, and it explains what the benchmark in this repository can and cannot support. The protocol is deliberately conservative. It is written for someone who has to defend a number in a paper, a specification or a safety case, not for someone who wants the quickest possible estimate.

entries.chapterTitle: Measuring a threshold without fooling yourself
entries.heading: 11.1 What is being estimated
entries.text: The infinite-volume threshold is A simulation has finite L, so it never observes . Instead it observes a pseudo-critical point p c(L), defined by a convention. Common conventions are: - the p at which the crossing probability (p,L) equals 1/2; - the p at which the susceptibility proxy (p,L) is maximal; - the crossing point of the Binder cumulant U 4=1- S^4 /(3 S^2 ^2) for two sizes; - the p at which the largest-cluster fraction S { }(p,L) equals a fixed fraction of the box. Each convention has a different finite-size correction. On the square lattice with bond percolation, the first is special: duality gives (1/2,L)=1/2 exactly for every L with free boundary conditions. That is a rare luxury, and it is why the square-lattice bond model is the calibration case for any new code. It is not a licence to use the same shortcut on another lattice. The differences between conventions are not cosmetic. If p c(L)=p c+aL^{-1/ }(1+bL^{- }+ ), then the coefficient a depends on the observable, while p c and do not. Two conventions that disagree by 10^{-2} at L=64 can agree to 10^{-4} after extrapolation, or can reveal a bug. Reporting the convention is part of reporting the number.

entries.chapterTitle: Measuring a threshold without fooling yourself
entries.heading: 11.2 Finite-size scaling, used as a test rather than a decoration
entries.text: Near p c, the scaling ansatz for an observable A is where y A is the scaling dimension of A and is the leading correction exponent. For the crossing probability y A=0, so the curves for different L should cross at p c and collapse when plotted against (p-p c)L^{1/ }. For S { }, y A=d f; for , y A= / . A collapse is evidence, not proof. It can be produced by adjusting three parameters to fit noise, especially when the range of L is small. Three safeguards make it informative: 1. Hold out a size. Fit on L L { }/2 and predict L { }. A collapse that only works when the largest size is included is a fit, not a test. 2. Show the residuals. A plot of residuals against the scaling variable exposes a trend that an overplotted collapse hides. 3. Report the window. The value of that minimises the collapse depends on the range of p used. Publish the range; do not publish only the minimum. The correction term matters. At L=32 to 128 on the square lattice, ignoring L^{- } can shift an extrapolated by several percent. The benchmark in this repository uses sizes up to 128 and reports the fit window with the result, but it is a teaching dataset, not a high-precision measurement.

entries.chapterTitle: Measuring a threshold without fooling yourself
entries.heading: 11.3 The Newman–Ziff sweep
entries.text: For bond percolation there is an algorithm that removes the outer loop over p. Draw one random ordering of the m edges. Add the edges one at a time. After k edges, the configuration is a sample from bond percolation at p=k/m, but the samples at different k are strongly correlated by construction. Maintain a union-find structure and the sum of squared cluster sizes. When an edge joins clusters of sizes a and b, the sum increases by 2ab. The largest cluster and the number of clusters are updated in O(1). The full sweep costs O(m\, (n)), where is the inverse Ackermann function, and it produces the whole curve \{S { }(k/m), (k/m)\} {k=0}^{m}. Two cautions. First, the curve from one edge order is one sample path, not an ensemble average; the visible smoothness comes from the monotone construction, not from averaging. Second, the samples at nearby p are almost identical, so the effective number of independent configurations is much smaller than the number of plotted points. Error bars computed as if each point were independent are far too small. The algorithm extends to site percolation by adding sites and their incident edges in a random order, but the bookkeeping is more delicate: an edge is active only when both endpoints have appeared. The JavaScript engine in this repository implements the bond version only.

entries.chapterTitle: Measuring a threshold without fooling yourself
entries.heading: 11.4 Uncertainty that survives review
entries.text: Three sources of error are usually conflated. Statistical error. For an indicator such as a crossing event, the standard error at n independent samples is { (1- )/n}. At =1/2 and n=1600, that is 0.0125 — larger than the differences between many published thresholds. For a cluster observable, the variance is dominated by the largest clusters; use a bootstrap over configurations, not a Gaussian formula. Finite-size error. This is a bias, not a variance. It is estimated by repeating the measurement at several L and extrapolating. The extrapolation is only as good as the assumed correction form. Report at least two fit forms and show that the conclusion is stable, or report the spread as part of the error. Systematic error. The lattice geometry, boundary conditions, the definition of a spanning cluster, the random-number generator, and the way ties are broken can all shift the answer. The cross-language parity tests in this repository exist because the last two are easy to get wrong and hard to see. A defensible statement has the form "we obtain p c=0.5927(3) from sizes L=64–512, with the crossing convention =1/2, a fit window p [0.58,0.60], and a correction exponent =1.5 fixed." A number without those qualifiers is a rumour.

entries.chapterTitle: Measuring a threshold without fooling yourself
entries.heading: 11.5 A protocol
entries.text: 1. Fix the model. Lattice, site or bond, boundary conditions, and the definition of spanning. Write them down before looking at data. 2. Calibrate on a solved case. Square-lattice bond percolation at p=1/2 must give a crossing rate consistent with 1/2 and each language implementation must agree exactly for the same seed. 3. Choose two observables. One indicator (crossing) and one cluster statistic (S { } or ). If they disagree on p c(L), you have a finite-size problem or a bug. 4. Use enough samples. Start with 10^4 crossing samples per size. At =1/2 this gives a standard error of about 0.5\%; state the target as a standard error and increase the sample until it is below the effect you want to claim. 5. Sweep L geometrically. At least four sizes spanning a factor of eight. A power law fitted to three points is a line through three points. 6. Fit with corrections. Use the ansatz of Section 11.2, hold out the largest size, and report the fit window. 7. Check the residuals and the conventions. A change of convention should move the estimate by less than the quoted error after extrapolation. 8. Publish the raw counts. The benchmark file in this repository stores n and hits for every point, so a reader can recompute the rate rather than trust a plotted curve.

entries.chapterTitle: Measuring a threshold without fooling yourself
entries.heading: 11.6 What the benchmark in this repository shows
entries.text: scripts/bench.cpp is a self-contained C++20 harness. It uses the shared xoshiro128 stream, the same lattice edge order as the libraries, and writes raw counts rather than fitted values. scripts/analyse bench.py adds the Cardy curve, a collapse fit and a one-arm slope, and records the seed and the generation date in data/benchmarks.json. The benchmark is designed to show the shape of a finite-size study, not to compete with dedicated high-precision work. The crossing experiment uses free boundaries and L \{32,64,128\}; the torus experiment uses L 128; the Cardy experiment uses a 96 H rectangle with H/W from 0.25 to 4. Every row carries its own sample count. The data view on the website reads the same file; if the file is missing, the page says so rather than inventing a curve. The important test is not whether the fitted p c lands on 0.5 to four decimals. It is whether the crossing rate at p=1/2 is statistically consistent with 1/2, whether the curves sharpen with L, and whether the same seed produces the same integer counts in C++, Julia, Python and JavaScript. Those are the checks that catch the errors which matter.

entries.chapterTitle: Measuring a threshold without fooling yourself
entries.heading: 11.7 Traps, in the order they usually appear
entries.text: Trap Symptom Fix --- --- --- Using one lattice size A threshold quoted to four decimals from L=64 Sweep L; extrapolate Treating correlated sweep points as independent Error bars shrinking as 1/ {m} Block/bootstrap by edge order Fitting a straight line on log–log axes An exponent that drifts with the window Include corrections; show residuals Confusing =1/2 with p c on an arbitrary lattice A biased threshold that looks precise Use the correct crossing convention Using the wrong spanning definition A crossing rate that is not comparable to the literature State the boundary arcs and the cluster criterion Comparing codes by mean only A bug that cancels in the average Compare integer counts for a fixed seed Quoting a numerical exponent as exact A "theorem" that changes in the next paper Label exact, numerical, or conjectural The last row is an editorial rule as much as a numerical one. The atlas marks exact results with ★ and labels numerical values with their source and precision; Chapter 14 records the corrections that this policy has forced.

entries.chapterTitle: Applications, and how to use the theory without abusing it
entries.heading: Applications, and how to use the theory without abusing it
entries.text: Percolation earns its keep in applications because it answers one question very well: given a random medium, is there a connected path across it? Everything else — the threshold value, the exponents, the finite-size corrections — is a refinement of that question. Most failed applications fail not because the mathematics is wrong but because the question being asked is not the one percolation answers.

entries.chapterTitle: Applications, and how to use the theory without abusing it
entries.heading: 12.1 A translation protocol
entries.text: Before writing any code, answer five questions. If any answer is "no" or "not sure", the model is not yet a percolation model. 1. What are the elements? Sites, bonds, or both? In a porous rock the pores are sites and the throats are bonds; in a composite the filler particles are sites and their contacts are bonds; in an epidemic the individuals are sites and the contacts are bonds. The choice changes the threshold, so it is not a detail. 2. What is the control parameter? Volume fraction, connectivity, occupancy, removal fraction — and is it the effective or the nominal one? Agglomeration, swelling, compression and measurement bias all move the effective value away from the nominal one. 3. What is the relevant connectivity? For transport it is usually the existence of a path; for mechanical integrity it is the existence of a load-bearing backbone; for epidemiology it is a path in a temporal contact network. These are different connectivities on the same graph, with different thresholds. 4. Which phase is the system in? If the answer is "near the threshold", then the response is dominated by the critical region and the answers are scale-dependent. If the answer is "far above", a mean-field or effective-medium estimate is usually enough and percolation adds little. 5. What is the sample size relative to the correlation length? If L/ is not large, finite-size effects are the signal, not the noise. This is a common failure mode in engineering applications. The protocol is deliberately conservative. A model that passes all five is a percolation model and can borrow the entire toolkit of this atlas. A model that fails one can still be useful, but it is an analogy, and analogies should not be used to quote a threshold.

entries.chapterTitle: Applications, and how to use the theory without abusing it
entries.heading: 12.2 Composites and electrodes
entries.text: Conductive composites. Insulating polymer plus conductive filler: the conductivity jumps when the filler volume fraction crosses the percolation threshold of the filler network. Three facts from the theory matter more than the exact threshold. First, shape beats quantity . The threshold scales roughly with the inverse aspect ratio for rods and with the inverse of the dimensionless, normalized excluded volume for plates, so high-aspect-ratio fillers (carbon nanotubes, graphene) percolate at fractions one or two orders of magnitude below spherical carbon black. The relevant geometric quantity is the average excluded volume, not the mass fraction. Second, dispersion is the control variable . The effective occupancy is the fraction of well-dispersed filler, not the nominal loading. Agglomerates reduce the effective p while increasing the nominal one, which is why two batches with identical formulation can sit on opposite sides of the threshold. This produces the bimodal performance distribution familiar to battery and composite engineers; it is a percolation effect, not a mixing-quality anecdote. Third, anisotropy follows processing . Alignment of anisotropic fillers changes the threshold in a direction-dependent way: the percolation threshold along the alignment direction drops, and perpendicular to it rises. A single scalar "threshold" is then meaningless; the correct object is a directional threshold tensor. Battery electrodes. A lithium iron phosphate cathode is a poor electronic conductor and needs a conductive additive (carbon black, carbon nanotubes) plus a carbon coating. The additive forms a percolating network; below the threshold the electrode is rate-limited by electronic transport, above it the extra additive displaces active material and reduces energy density. The engineering problem is therefore a narrow window just above the threshold, and the theory's contribution is to explain why the window is narrow: the conductivity grows as a power law above p c, so a small change in loading produces a large change in conductivity only near the threshold, exactly where the batch-to-batch scatter is largest. The same structure appears in solid electrolytes (ionic percolation through grain boundaries), in fuel-cell catalyst layers (electronic and ionic networks must both percolate, a two-phase percolation problem), and in thermal interface materials.

entries.chapterTitle: Applications, and how to use the theory without abusing it
entries.heading: 12.3 Porous media and hydrology
entries.text: In a porous rock the pore space is the site graph and the throats are the bonds. As water saturation decreases, the water-filled subgraph thins and at a critical saturation the hydraulic conductance drops to zero. The percolation threshold sets the irreducible saturation; the power-law conductivity above it sets the shape of the relative-permeability curve. Two refinements are essential in practice. The pore-size distribution makes the occupation probability site-dependent, so the relevant model is correlated or weighted percolation, and the threshold is set by the largest throats that must be invaded (invasion percolation). And the geometry is often dual-porosity: fractures percolate at a much lower density than the matrix, and the two networks exchange fluid. A single p c is then not a material constant but a function of the measurement direction and scale. The application to contaminant transport is the one with the clearest engineering consequence: near the threshold, first-passage times are heavy-tailed, so the mean arrival time is not a useful risk measure. Use quantiles.

entries.chapterTitle: Applications, and how to use the theory without abusing it
entries.heading: 12.4 Epidemiology
entries.text: For an SIR epidemic on a static contact network, retain each edge independently with the per-contact transmission probability T. The final size is the giant component of the resulting percolation graph. That is an exact statement in the infinite-population limit for a configuration-model network; it avoids the circular phrase "delete the vertices that escape", since which vertices escape is precisely what the construction determines. It gives the random-immunisation threshold as where = k^2 / k is the Molloy–Reed ratio. For homogeneous mixing R 0 T k , and for T 1 the heterogeneous expression reduces to 1-1/( -1). The heterogeneity matters: for a network with a heavy-tailed degree distribution, the fraction that must be immune is larger than the homogeneous formula suggests, and targeted immunity of high-degree vertices is far more efficient than random immunity. Two warnings. The mapping assumes a static network and a Markovian epidemic; for temporal networks with bursty contacts the percolation threshold is replaced by a temporal connectivity threshold, and the two can differ by a large factor. And the herd-immunity threshold is a statement about the final size in an infinite population, not about the peak or the time course, which require the dynamics that percolation deliberately discards.

entries.chapterTitle: Applications, and how to use the theory without abusing it
entries.heading: 12.5 Infrastructure and cascades
entries.text: The 2010 result on interdependent networks (Chapter 10) is the theoretical basis for the modern view that coupled infrastructures fail abruptly. The engineering translation has three parts. Coupling topology matters more than coupling strength. A one-to-one dependency between a power grid and its communication network turns a continuous transition into a first-order one. Partial coupling, or multiple redundant dependencies, restores a continuous transition. This is a design choice, not a law of nature. The cascade is a sequence of giant-component computations. Each round removes the vertices that lost their support, recomputes the giant component, and repeats. The number of rounds is small (typically under ten) and the total loss is much larger than the initial shock. Any mitigation that shortens the cascade — buffering, islanding, redundant control — acts by keeping the surviving set above the threshold of the next round. Metrics must be cascade-aware. A network that is robust to random failures at the single-layer level can be fragile when coupled, so a robustness audit that examines each layer separately is not merely imprecise; it can give the wrong sign. Wildfire is a natural percolation problem with the same structure: fuel connectivity is the control parameter, and the transition from exponentially truncated fire sizes to power-law fire sizes is the percolation transition. Firebreaks work by lowering the effective connectivity below the threshold, and the practical lesson is the same as in the composite case: the change in outcome per unit change in the control parameter is largest near the threshold, so a firebreak density that is "almost enough" is the worst place to be.

entries.chapterTitle: Applications, and how to use the theory without abusing it
entries.heading: 12.6 Imaging, sensing, and tissue
entries.text: Image segmentation. Thresholding an image and taking the largest connected component is percolation with a spatially correlated field. The choice of threshold is the choice of p, and the "right" threshold is the one at which the structure of interest percolates while the noise does not. The percolation picture explains why a single global threshold fails on heterogeneous images and why hysteresis (two thresholds, one for growth and one for merging) works better: it is an explicit finite-size correction to a critical phenomenon. Wireless sensor networks. Coverage and connectivity are different questions. Coverage is the smooth area fraction of the union of disks (a Boolean model); connectivity is a continuum percolation problem with its own threshold, c 1.128 in two dimensions for the reduced density =n r^2 (Mertens and Moore 2012). Confusing the two produces optimistic deployment rules: coverage is a statement about the union of disks, while connectivity is a statement about a spanning cluster, and at finite density one can have high coverage without a spanning cluster. Tissue engineering. A porous scaffold must have connected pores for cell migration and vascularisation. Below the pore-connectivity threshold, cells remain at the surface and the construct fails to vascularise; above it, penetration is rapid. The threshold depends on pore-size distribution and on cell size, which makes it a weighted percolation problem again.

entries.chapterTitle: Applications, and how to use the theory without abusing it
entries.heading: 12.7 Four case studies, with what the model does not give
entries.text: Case 1: carbon-black polymer composite. Percolation says the conductivity jump occurs at a filler fraction set by filler geometry and dispersion. It does not give the absolute conductivity, which depends on tunnelling between particles, contact resistance, and polymer morphology. Use percolation for the threshold and the power-law exponent; use a transport model for the amplitude. Case 2: LFP cathode. Percolation says the rate capability collapses below a critical additive loading and that the window above it is narrow. It does not give the electrochemical impedance, the lithium diffusion coefficient, or the calendering effect on particle contact. Use percolation to bracket the formulation window, then measure. Case 3: measles vaccination. Percolation gives the herd-immunity threshold for a homogeneous mixing model and its correction for heterogeneous contact networks. It does not give the vaccination coverage actually achieved, the timing of the campaign, or the behaviour of the contact network during a school holiday. Use it to set a target, not to predict an outbreak. Case 4: coupled power/communication cascade. Percolation predicts the existence of a first-order transition and the scaling of the cascade size. It does not predict which line trips first. Use it to compare topologies and to justify redundancy; do not use it to forecast a specific blackout. The pattern in all four is the same: percolation gives thresholds, scaling and qualitative transitions with remarkable reliability, and gives amplitudes and dynamics poorly or not at all. An application that respects the division of labour is useful; one that quotes a threshold as a material constant is not.

entries.chapterTitle: The cross-disciplinary map, and what is still open
entries.heading: The cross-disciplinary map, and what is still open
entries.text: Percolation is a small model with a large catchment area. This chapter maps the connections that are exact, the ones that are approximate, and the ones that are merely metaphorical — and then lists the problems that are actually open, in the order in which they look tractable.

entries.chapterTitle: The cross-disciplinary map, and what is still open
entries.heading: 13.1 Exact correspondences
entries.text: Spin models. The random-cluster representation (Chapter 9) makes the q-state Potts model and percolation the same measure at different values of a parameter. At q=1 the percolation probability is the Potts magnetisation, and the phase transitions coincide. This is an identity, not an analogy, and it is the reason percolation exponents can be computed with spin-model technology. Random graphs. The Erdős–Rényi giant component is percolation on the complete graph; the configuration-model giant component is percolation on a random multigraph. The Molloy–Reed criterion is the exact statement, and it is the same branching-process computation as the Bethe lattice. Electrical networks. The link between percolation and resistor networks is exact at the level of the random-cluster model with wired boundary conditions: the effective conductance has a variational (Dirichlet) representation determined by the cluster structure, and it vanishes exactly when no open cluster connects the electrodes. The scaling of the conductivity is a well-defined critical exponent t: high-precision simulations give t 1.299 in two dimensions (Grassberger 1999) and t 2.0 in three dimensions. These are numerical values, not conformal-field-theory theorems. The relation t= (d-2+ ) defines the resistance exponent , and the failure of the naive Einstein relation is the "anomalous" part. Epidemics. The final size of an SIR epidemic on a static network is the giant component of the percolation graph — the network with each edge retained with probability equal to the per-contact transmission probability. This is exact in the infinite-population limit. Coupled networks. The cascade in interdependent networks is a sequence of giant-component computations, so each step is exact; the mean-field solution of the sequence is approximate but the first-order character is robust.

entries.chapterTitle: The cross-disciplinary map, and what is still open
entries.heading: 13.2 Approximate and contested correspondences
entries.text: Glass transitions. Dynamic heterogeneity in supercooled liquids is often described as "dynamical percolation" of mobile regions. The phenomenology is suggestive and the exponents sometimes match, but there is no derivation of the dynamics from a percolation model. Treat the correspondence as a metaphor with predictive value for scaling collapses, not as an identity. Neural criticality. Avalanches in cortical tissue show power-law size distributions, and branching-process models (which are percolation on a tree) reproduce them. The identification of a critical brain with a percolation critical point is contested: the exponents are not universal across preparations, and the measured networks are small enough that finite-size effects dominate. Machine learning. The "emergence" of capabilities with scale, the sparsity threshold at which pruning destroys a network, and the connectivity of random feature maps have all been described in percolation language. Some of these are rigorous (pruning thresholds in random sparse networks are k-core thresholds); most are analogies. The distinction matters, because a percolation analogy predicts a sharp threshold where the actual phenomenon may be smooth. Financial contagion. Interbank networks do exhibit cascade behaviour and the interdependent-network machinery applies to the extent that the balance-sheet constraints really are "survive only if your counterparty survives". In practice the constraints are partial, delayed and weighted, so the quantitative thresholds are not transferable. The qualitative lesson — coupling creates first-order fragility — survives. Climate tipping points. Spatial connectivity of sea ice, vegetation and ocean circulation has been analysed with percolation. The analogy is useful for detecting early warning signals (critical slowing down), but the systems are forced, non-stationary and finite, which violates the model's assumptions.

entries.chapterTitle: The cross-disciplinary map, and what is still open
entries.heading: 13.3 A checklist for a cross-disciplinary claim
entries.text: Whenever a paper says "X is a percolation problem", ask: 1. What is the graph, explicitly? 2. What is the random element, and is it independent? 3. What is the control parameter, and can it be varied independently of the others? 4. Which connectivity is meant, and is it the one that controls the phenomenon? 5. Is the system in the critical region, and is the system size larger than the correlation length? 6. Which predictions are specific to percolation (a threshold, an exponent, a universality class) rather than generic consequences of connectivity? A claim that answers all six is a scientific contribution. A claim that answers none is a metaphor, which may still be useful for teaching but should not be used to make predictions.

entries.chapterTitle: The cross-disciplinary map, and what is still open
entries.heading: 13.4 Open problems
entries.text: The list is ordered from "likely to fall in the next decade" to "may be out of reach". Each entry says why it matters. 1. Conformal invariance for non-triangular planar lattices. Smirnov's theorem is specific to the triangular lattice. For the square-lattice site problem, the scaling limit is believed to be conformally invariant and SLE 6; the proof is missing. This is the last piece of the universality puzzle in two dimensions, and it is the most concrete open problem in the field. 2. Critical exponents in 3 d 5. The numerical values are excellent and the rigorous values are absent. A proof of mean-field behaviour down to d=7 would still leave the physical dimensions open, but it would be a major step. The obstacle is the divergence of the lace expansion below d=11. 3. The d=6 logarithmic corrections. The exponents are mean-field at d=6, but the logarithms' coefficients are not rigorously known in full. This is a technically hard but well-posed problem. 4. Classification of higher-order percolation transitions. On simplicial complexes, the transition type depends on the definition of connectivity (Betti-number connectivity, k-th order connectivity, Euler characteristic). Is there a classification theorem? At present there is a zoo of numerical behaviours and no unified theory. 5. Stability of first-order transitions under partial coupling. The 2.4554 constant is for fully coupled Poisson layers. For realistic partial, weighted and time-varying coupling, the location and even the order of the transition are open. 6. Optimal attack and defence. Given a degree distribution and a budget, what removal sequence minimises the giant component, and what edge additions maximise robustness? This is a combinatorial optimisation problem with a percolation objective; the mean-field answers are known, the finite-size and adversarial versions are not. 7. Temporal percolation. Real connectivity is time-dependent: a path must exist and be traversable within a time window. The theory of temporal percolation is young, and the appropriate scaling theory is not settled. 8. Algorithmic complexity of percolation quantities. Computing the percolation probability or the reliability polynomial of a given finite graph is P-hard in general; the complexity of recovering the infinite-volume threshold from finite data, and the planar case in particular, are separate questions. The connection to the Tutte polynomial suggests a complexity classification, but it has not been worked out for percolation thresholds specifically. 9. Quantum error correction thresholds. The threshold theorem for surface codes is well established; the optimal thresholds for general code families, and the behaviour under correlated noise, are open. The percolation analogy is exact for some decoding problems and only heuristic for others. 10. Percolation in learning systems. Whether the sparsity thresholds observed in pruning and the "emergence" phenomena have a percolation description that is more than an analogy is genuinely unknown. The question is worth asking carefully, because the answer determines whether the thresholds can be predicted or only observed.

entries.chapterTitle: The cross-disciplinary map, and what is still open
entries.heading: 13.5 What this atlas is for
entries.text: The atlas is a working document, not a monument. Every chapter is a Markdown file with a stable id; every result marked ★ has a proof or a proof sketch in its chapter; every number has a source. If you find an error, the errata table in the next chapter is where it should go, with the date and the correction. That is the only way a reference of this kind stays useful after its authors stop looking at it.

entries.heading: Sources, corrections, and maintenance
entries.text: A reference work is only as good as its provenance. This final chapter records where the claims come from, which claims are exact and which are numerical, what has been corrected in this edition, and how to maintain the repository without breaking the guarantees that make it useful.

entries.heading: 14.1 Editorial rules
entries.text: Five rules govern the content. 1. Primary sources for results. A theorem is cited to the paper or book that proves it, not to a review that mentions it. Where a result has a long history, the original and the standard modern reference are both given. 2. Exact, numerical, or conjectural. Every exponent and threshold carries one of these labels. A numerical value is quoted with the precision its source supports, not with the precision of a plotting tool. A conjecture is called a conjecture even when it is universally believed. 3. No silent rounding. Where a value is rounded, the source's uncertainty is preserved. Where two sources disagree in the last digit, the conservative value is used and the disagreement is noted. 4. No invented citations. If a claim cannot be traced to a source, it is either removed or explicitly marked as a heuristic argument. The bibliography in the Sources view is generated from content/references.json; every entry there has a DOI or a stable publisher URL. 5. Corrections are public. A correction is dated and described in Section 14.3. Removing a wrong statement without recording it makes the next reader repeat the error. The prose is written to be read by a person. Mathematical notation is standard; undefined jargon is explained at first use; rhetorical flourishes are kept to a minimum. The three language editions are authored, not machine-translated at runtime. Technical terms follow the glossary in docs/EDITORIAL.md so that a search for "threshold" finds the same concept in every edition.

entries.heading: 14.2 How to read a citation
entries.text: The bibliography uses author–year keys in the text and full entries in the Sources view. For a journal article the entry gives authors, title, journal, volume, pages, year and DOI. For a book it gives the edition actually used. For a computational result it gives the algorithm, the sample sizes and the seed where those are part of the claim. Two conventions are worth stating. First, the year is the year of the version that was actually consulted. A preprint that appeared in 2016 and a journal version that appeared in 2017 are different objects; the entry says which one. Second, a DOI resolves to the publisher's record, not to a copy of the paper. The atlas does not host copyrighted PDFs.

entries.heading: 14.3 Corrections in this edition
entries.text: The following errors were found in earlier drafts of this atlas and in the first release of its code. They are listed with the correction and, where relevant, the numerical consequence. Where Earlier statement Correction --- --- --- --- 1 Coupled-network cascade, Chapter 10, lab, C++/Julia/Python/JS library and benchmark Layer A and layer B were each pruned to their own giant component, without intersecting the two surviving sets. With one-to-one coupling a vertex survives only if it is in both giant components. The round is an intersection. The parity probe changed from 0.668 to 0.5306666666666666 for seed 11, and the benchmark curve is lower near p c. 2 Random-cluster chapter The Ising critical point on the square lattice was placed at p=1/2. The q=2 self-dual point is p c= 2/(1+ 2)=0.585786 . The value 1/2 is the q=1 percolation point. 3 Random-cluster chapter Duality was described as p 1-p at every q. On the square lattice the self-dual curve is p= q/(1+ q); p 1-p is the q=1 special case. 4 Conductivity discussion, Chapter 13 The two-dimensional conductivity exponent t 1.299 was called exactly known. It is a high-precision numerical value (Grassberger 1999), not a conformal-field-theory theorem. 5 Continuum lab and Chapter 12 Coverage was described as having a threshold at =0, contrasted with connectivity at c 1.128. Coverage is the smooth function 1-e^{- }; it has no threshold. The percolation threshold of the Poisson disk model is the separate quantity c 1.128 (area fraction 0.676). 6 Universality discussion, Chapters 6 and 13 "Every periodic planar lattice has the same exponents" was stated as a theorem. The theorem is for the triangular lattice and its star–triangle relatives. The general planar case is a conjecture supported by numerics. 7 Sharpness chapter Continuity at p c was said to be open only for 3 d 5. It is known in d=2 and in sufficiently high dimensions, and open in the intermediate range; the chapter now states it that way. 8 Threshold table, 3D values The BCC/FCC/diamond values were attributed to Lorenz–Ziff (1998). Lorenz–Ziff determined the sc, fcc and bcc bond thresholds; the site and diamond values are quoted from van der Marck (1997), and the sc values from Wang et al. (2013). 9 Chapter 12 The heterogeneous herd-immunity threshold was written as 1-1/( -1) without the transmissibility. The general form is v c=1-1/R 0 with R 0=T( -1); the simpler expression is the T=1 special case. 10 Chapter 13 "Peridemic graph" and a claim that exact percolation thresholds of finite graphs are P-hard. The term is corrected to "percolation graph". The complexity sentence now distinguishes finite-graph reliability ( P-hard) from recovering an infinite-volume threshold, which is a different problem. 11 Benchmark harness The rejection limit in scripts/bench.cpp was computed in 32-bit arithmetic and wrapped to zero when the stub count divided 2^{32}, making the shuffle loop forever. The limit is now computed in 64-bit arithmetic. The four libraries were not affected; their rejection samplers already used 64-bit or exact integer arithmetic. 12 Cardy formula, Chapter 7, Cardy lab, four libraries and golden probes The hypergeometric was evaluated at argument - ; the resulting curve gave (0.1)=0.2585, (10)=0.7414 and was much too flat. The correct argument is the elliptic modulus m solving =K(m)/K(1-m). Correct values: (0.1)=4.03949 10^{-5}, (1)=0.5, (10)=0.9999596. The libraries, lab, tests and golden values were updated. The first correction was not a typo in the prose; it was an algorithmic error, and it survived because the wrong algorithm still produced a plausible curve. The Cardy correction was a formula error with a similarly large numerical effect. The lesson is recorded in Chapter 11: compare integer counts for a fixed seed, not just the shape of a plot.

entries.heading: 14.4 Reproducing the numbers
entries.text: The full pipeline is: make bench writes data/raw bench.json; the analyser writes data/benchmarks.json and prints the collapse fit and the one-arm slope. The website reads content/manifest.json, content/search.json and data/benchmarks.json. None of these generated files should be edited by hand. The parity probes in data/golden/parity.json are the contract between the four libraries. They cover a crossing count, a Newman–Ziff checkpoint triple, a configuration-model component size and a coupled-network cascade fraction. The random-stream vectors in data/golden/rng-seed42.json pin the generator itself. A change to the random stream, the edge order or the consumption order is a breaking change and requires new golden files, a version bump and a note in this chapter.

entries.heading: 14.5 Maintaining the atlas
entries.text: Adding a chapter. Create content/en/NN-slug.md, content/zh/NN-slug.md and content/de/NN-slug.md with the same id, order and structure. Add the references to content/references.json. Run scripts/build content.py; it fails if a language is missing or an order is duplicated. Add the chapter to the test matrix if it introduces a computed number. Adding a laboratory. Put the engine in assets/js/engine/ only if it is part of the shared contract. Put the page in assets/js/labs/, register it in LABS, and localise at least the title, the lead, every control label and the readout captions. A lab that only works in English is not finished. Adding a language. Add the language code to LANGS, add a content directory, add a UI string table, and extend scripts/build content.py. The layout must be checked at 1280, 1440 and 1920 pixels; German labels are longer than English and Chinese labels are shorter, and a layout that only fits one language is not a layout. Updating a result. Change the Markdown source, not the generated JSON. If the result affects a code path, add a regression test first. If it changes a published number, add a row to Section 14.3 and bump the minor version. Review cadence. Once a year, check every DOI, re-run the benchmark on the current compiler, and compare the new raw counts with the previous record. A change in counts with the same seed is either a compiler bug, a platform-dependent floating-point path, or a change in the algorithm. All three are worth knowing about.

entries.heading: 14.6 Licence and citation
entries.text: The text is released under CC BY 4.0 and the code under MIT; see LICENSE and LICENSE-CONTENT. Citation metadata is in CITATION.cff. When citing a specific result, cite the original source as well as the atlas; the atlas is a guide to the literature, not a substitute for it. The atlas is maintained as a static site with no server-side dependencies. That is a deliberate choice: it can be archived, mirrored and read offline, and it will still work when the build tool of the month has been forgotten.

entries.heading: 渗流是什么
entries.text: 一杯咖啡就是一个随机介质。水之所以能穿过压实的咖啡渣层，是因为其中一些通道是开的、另一些是闭的；水走哪条路，取决于渣层的几何结构，而不是水自身的任何随机性。1957 年，Broadbent 与 Hammersley 把这一图景写成数学，并借用拉丁语 percolare （渗过）将其命名为 percolation （渗流）。他们的用意既在技术，也在哲学：扩散理论中介质固定，行走的粒子随机；渗流中介质随机，而一旦介质被抽取出来，穿过它的流动便完全确定。 仅凭这一次反转，便生出了一整个领域。令图中每个位点或每条键以概率 p 独立地取为开，然后问一个只答是或否的问题：开元素中是否存在无穷连通分量？答案在某个 p 值处发生质变。在该值附近，几何变得标度不变，描述它的诸量服从幂律，而幂律的指数不依赖于图的微观细节。这是一个没有温度、没有能量、也没有哈密顿量的相变——只有连通性。

entries.heading: 一段话讲完模型
entries.text: 设 G=(V,E) 是可数无限、局部有限、连通的图，并取定一个原点 0 V。给每个位点（位点渗流）或每条键（键渗流）配一个均值为 p 的独立 Bernoulli 变量。开元素构成一个随机子图，其连通分量就是 开团簇 。记 C 0 为包含原点的团簇，并定义 本图册后面的全部内容，都只是对这两行的细化。函数 是序参量，p c 是临界概率；真正有意思的命题，说的都是 p p c 与 p p c 时会发生什么。

entries.heading: 六个可观测量
entries.text: 几乎整个理论都靠六个量支撑。值得把它们的定义一次固定下来：不同领域对它们的归一化方式不同，文献中一半的混乱其实只是记账方式不同。 渗流概率。 (p)= {P} p(0 )。 两点函数。 p(x,y)= {P} p(x y)，其中 p(x)= p(0,x)。这是连通性核；在可迁图上它只依赖于 x-y。 团簇尺寸分布。 n(p)= {P} p( C 0 =n)，n< ，并记 = 。 磁化率。 (p)= {n 1} n\, n(p)= {E} p [ C 0 ;\ C 0 < ]。这是原点所在团簇的平均尺寸，其中无穷团簇不计入。它在 p p c 时发散；这一发散是临界性最干净利落的数值信号。 关联长度。 (p)^{-1}= {n }- 1n p(0,n e 1)，即沿坐标轴方向连通性衰减的指数速率。无论从哪一侧趋近，p p c 时它都发散。 横穿概率。 在有限盒子 上， (p)= {P} p( {open left–right crossing of } )。这是有限尺度研究真正测量的量：它是一个指示量，阈值随 L 变得锐利，而且不需要无穷格子。 第六个量是单位位点上的团簇数密度 n s(p)= {P} p( C 0 =s)/s，它是标度理论的天然对象；第 6 章会用到它， 之所以存在也正源于此。

entries.heading: 为什么一个参数就够了
entries.anchor: 为什么一个参数就够了
entries.text: 人们很容易认为，结构如此贫乏的模型不可能产生任何普适的东西。事实恰恰相反，原因在于尺度分离。在 p c 附近，关联长度 远大于格子间距，因此在团簇“决定”自己是否无穷之前，键的微观排布早已被反复平均掉了。普适性说的是：在这一极限下，微观模型只有少数特征存留下来——维数，以及约束大尺度几何的对称性（旋转与反射不变性，对渗流而言还有开与闭之间的颜色对称性）。 这种经济性的代价是：模型 只在单一的点上临界 ，因而在数值上十分娇气。在 p c 处，相关尺度就是系统尺寸本身，有限尺度效应是幂律型的而非指数型的，朴素的拟合会给出有偏的指数。第 11 章专门讨论如何把这件事做对。

entries.heading: 图景的五个层次
entries.text: 这门学问通常是一层一层教的，而一次看全整个层次结构会很有帮助。 1. 局部连通性。 固定 p 时，盒子里有许多大小不一的团簇；尺寸分布正是研究对象。 2. 阈值。 在无限可迁图上，存在唯一的 p c (0,1) 使定性行为发生改变。存在性容易证明，确定其位置却很难。 3. 临界标度。 在 p c 附近，各可观测量按 p-p c 或系统尺寸的幂次变化，其指数是普适的。 4. 几何极限。 在二维，临界团簇的标度极限具有共形不变性，界面收敛到 SLE 6。这是唯一一个极限已被完全理解的维数。 5. 转译。 Ising 模型、Potts 模型、随机图、传染病、电阻网络、纠错码和网络鲁棒性，都可以写成渗流问题，有时是精确的等价，有时只是类比。区分这两者，是本图册反复出现的主题。

entries.heading: 里程碑
entries.text: 三个结果足以让初来者找到方向。正方格子上，键渗流的 p c=1/2 是精确值（Kesten 1980）。三角格子上，位点渗流的 p c=1/2 也是精确值，其证明只需一个简短的星–三角论证（第 4 章）。对三角格子及其星–三角亲属，二维临界指数是精确已知的： =5/36， =43/18， =4/3， =91/5， =5/24，d f=91/48。三维的阈值与指数都没有精确已知值；最佳数值为 0.4181， 0.8764，d f 2.5229，误差棒在第三位小数。六维以上（d 6），平均场值 = =1， =1/2， =2， =0，d f=4 严格成立；在 d=6 处则带有对数修正。 精确结果与中间维度之间的空隙，正是这个领域诚实的形状：二维精确，六维以上严格，中间只能靠数值。

entries.heading: 如何阅读本图册
entries.text: 如果你想要直觉，读这一章和第 4 章，然后打开 Lattice 实验台，看横穿概率如何随 L 增大而变锐。 如果你想要严格的核心，按顺序读第 3–5 章（单调性与存在性、对偶与精确阈值、锐性与唯一性），再读第 7 章了解二维极限。 如果你是为应用而来，第 10 章和第 12 章分别讲网络与材料，第 11 章则是数值方法，它防止一项应用得出看似合理却错误的阈值。 如果你想核查某个论断：凡是完整证明的定理都标有 ★，每个数值都注明来源与精度，第 14 章则为证明编索引、记录本版的更正，并列出全书用到的文献。

entries.heading: 一段简史
entries.text: 渗流的历史异常干净：有一篇确定的开山论文，一个确定的黄金时代，以及二维问题的一个确定解决。以下是一条附有原始文献的时间线，每一条说法都可追溯。

entries.heading: 1957：奠基论文
entries.text: S. R. Broadbent and J. M. Hammersley, Percolation processes: I. Crystals and mazes , Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 53(3), 629–641. 该文引入模型，把它与扩散区分开，并提出那个定义整个领域的问题：临界概率是否存在？他们举的例子包括：气体在随机排列的阻塞通道中扩散，疾病在果园中传播，以及流体在多孔固体中渗流。开、闭、团簇、渗流概率这一套词汇，都出自他们。 配套短文 J. M. Hammersley, Percolation processes: II. The connective constant , 同卷, 642–645，讨论一维链与 Bethe 格子。在度为 z 的树上，阈值是 1/(z-1)，这是第一个精确的非平凡值，至今仍是平均场理论的几何化身。

entries.heading: 1960–1980：正方格子
entries.text: T. E. Harris, A lower bound for the critical probability in a certain percolation process , Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 56 (1960), 13–20，证明了 {Z}^2 上 (1/2)=0，即 p c 1/2。论证把开横穿与闭横穿的平面对偶性，同 p=1/2 处的颜色对称性结合起来；这两个想法此后都成了常备工具。 M. F. Sykes and J. W. Essam, Exact critical percolation probabilities for site and bond problems in two dimensions , J. Math. Phys. 5 (1964), 1117，引入匹配方法，得到三角格子与蜂窝格子键阈值的闭式。他们的路线经过星–三角变换；第 4 章正确复现了这一代数推导，并逐步核验。 L. Russo, A note on percolation , Z. Wahrsch. Verw. Gebiete 43 (1978), 39–48，以及 P. D. Seymour and D. J. A. Welsh, Percolation probabilities on the square lattice , Ann. Discrete Math. 3 (1978), 227–245，各自独立证明了盒子横穿不等式，使二维渗流变得可处理。RSW 引理几乎是每一个二维严格结果的发动机，包括两年后 Kesten 的定理。 H. Kesten, The critical probability of bond percolation on the square lattice equals 1/2 , Comm. Math. Phys. 74 (1980), 41–59，补上了这道缺口。证明冗长而技术化。Bollobás 与 Riordan（2006）利用锐阈值技术给出了一条短得多的路线。

entries.heading: 1970 年代–1980 年代：临界现象
entries.text: 把渗流转译成临界现象语言的工作，与 P.-G. de Gennes, On a relation between percolation theory and the elasticity of gels , J. Physique Lettres 37 (1976), L1–L2，以及 Stauffer 学派联系在一起。D. Stauffer and A. Aharony, Introduction to Percolation Theory (Taylor & Francis, 2nd ed. 1994)，固定了如今人人使用的记号 , , , , ，并教会了一代人从 Monte Carlo 数据拟合指数——有时过于乐观，第 11 章试图纠正这一积习。 在严格理论方面，H. Kesten, Percolation Theory for Mathematicians (Birkhäuser, 1982)，把这门学问确立为概率论的一个分支。M. Aizenman and D. J. Barsky, Sharpness of the phase transition in percolation models , Comm. Math. Phys. 108 (1987), 489–526，证明了 p c 以下的指数衰减；M. V. Menshikov 独立证明了相应结果（1986–87）。Burton–Keane 唯一性定理（1989）补全了超临界相的定性图景。

entries.heading: 1986–1992：高维与共形场论
entries.text: M. Aizenman and R. Fernández, On the critical behavior of the magnetization in high dimensional Ising models , J. Stat. Phys. 44 (1986), 393，以及 T. Hara and G. Slade, Mean-field critical behaviour for percolation in high dimensions , Comm. Math. Phys. 128 (1990), 333–391，用 lace 展开证明充分高维下的平均场行为。该方法是非微扰的，至今仍是超越上临界维数后通往临界指数的唯一严格途径。目前最近邻键渗流的维数阈值为 d 11（Fitzner and van der Hofstad, 2017），这一结果建立在 Hara 与 Slade 的 d 19 结果以及后来对展开的改进之上。 与此同时，J. L. Cardy, Critical percolation in finite geometries , J. Phys. A 25 (1992), L201，用共形场论预测了矩形的精确横穿概率。R. Langlands, P. Pouliot and Y. Saint-Aubin, Conformal invariance in two-dimensional percolation , Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 30 (1994), 1–61，对这一预测做了数值检验，并把背后的猜想归功于 Aizenman。

entries.heading: 2001：二维革命
entries.text: S. Smirnov, Critical percolation in the plane: conformal invariance, Cardy's formula, scaling limits , C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Sér. I Math. 333 (2001), 239–244，证明了三角格子上临界位点渗流的 Cardy 公式。这个证明短到一个下午就能读完，却又深到改变了整个学科：它把探索界面的连续极限认定为一个共形不变的对象。 G. F. Lawler, O. Schramm and W. Werner, Values of Brownian intersection exponents I, II , Acta Math. 187 (2001), 237–273 and 275–308，及其后续工作，把界面极限认定为 SLE 6，并导出了精确的指数集合。Cardy → Smirnov → SLE 这条链条，是继 Ising 模型之后二维临界模型最完整的解。

entries.heading: 2000 年代：网络
entries.text: R. Cohen, K. Erez, D. ben-Avraham and S. Havlin, Resilience of the Internet to random breakdowns , Phys. Rev. Lett. 85 (2000), 4626，以及 D. S. Callaway, M. E. J. Newman, S. H. Strogatz and D. J. Watts, Network robustness and fragility: percolation on random graphs , Phys. Rev. Lett. 85 (2000), 5468，把渗流带进了网络科学。Molloy–Reed 判据——在 M. Molloy and B. Reed, A critical point for random graphs with a given degree sequence , Random Structures & Algorithms 6 (1995), 161–180 中已具雏形——成了标准工具。 S. V. Buldyrev, R. Parshani, G. Paul, H. E. Stanley and S. Havlin, Catastrophic cascade of failures in interdependent networks , Nature 464 (2010), 1025–1028，表明把两个网络耦合起来，会把连续相变变成不连续相变。这一结果是“渗流相变的 类型 可以成为设计变量”的最清楚例子。

entries.heading: 2010 年代–2020 年代
entries.text: 严格的高维纲领推进到了 d 11，并证明了三角条件在该维数范围内成立；三维问题仍只能依靠数值。单纯复形上的高阶渗流、时间网络与多层网络上的渗流，以及量子纠错码的渗流阈值，是当前活跃的前沿。第 13 章按“看起来可处理的先后”列出未解问题。 有两处年代惯例值得点明。Aizenman–Barsky 的锐性论文常被引作 1986 年，因为该年它以预印本形式流传；期刊卷册的年份是 1987。另外，目前的高维阈值是 d 11，而不是二手文献中仍能见到的旧值 d 19。第 14 章记录这两处更正。

entries.heading: 单调性与阈值的存在性

entries.chapterTitle: 单调性与阈值的存在性
entries.heading: 3.6 单调性给不出的东西
entries.text: 单调性说的是 在图固定的前提下改变 p ，对改变图本身只字未提。加边会降低 p c；把每条边细分，相当于把概率为 p 的开键换成两个串联的键，于是键阈值移到 {p c}，反而升高。“连接越多，阈值越低”这一直觉，对加边是可靠的，对任意的图操作则不然。第 11 章列出由此产生的陷阱。 第二个局限：FKG 是不等式，不是恒等式。它只给出关联的符号，不给出关联的大小；要做定量工作（例如 RSW 常数），需要的是真正的横穿估计，其精细程度高得多。

entries.heading: 对偶、匹配与精确阈值
entries.text: 平面对偶是产生精确阈值的主要工具，它分两步走：先把关于开横穿的命题转换为关于闭横穿的命题，再用对称性论证把临界点钉在自对偶值上。在正方格子上，这两步给出 p c=1/2。在三角格子与蜂窝格子上，还需要第二样东西：星–三角变换。推导见 4.4 节；那里也会说明那个看似合理、却给出错误根的代数捷径。

entries.heading: 4.1 匹配图与横穿引理
entries.text: 定义 4.1。 设 G 是嵌入平面、面局部有限的图。 匹配图 G^ 在 G 的每个面内有一个顶点，并且对 G 的每条边有一条跨越该边的边，连接与该边相邻的两个面。若作为平面图有 G^ G，则称 G 是 自对偶 的。正方格子自对偶；三角格子与蜂窝格子互为匹配图。 引理 4.2（横穿对偶，★）。 设 n=[-n,n]^2， n^ 为匹配的正方形。对 n 上的每个键构型 ，下列两件事恰有一件成立： - A：存在 n 的一条开左右横穿； - B^ ：存在 n^ 的一条闭上下横穿。 证明。 把 n 的每条键染成开或闭，并按“原键开则对偶键闭、原键闭则对偶键开”的规则画出 n^ 的对偶键。于是两族键构成一对互补的平面对偶。 至多一件。 设 A 与 B^ 同时成立。开左右路径 P 与闭上下对偶路径 Q 必在某条原边 e 处相交：两条路径作为平面曲线相交，而水平原路径与竖直对偶路径的交叉恰好发生在一条边上。在该处，e 是开的（因为 P 用了它），又是闭的（因为 Q 用了它的对偶），矛盾。 至少一件。 设 A 不成立。考虑从盒子左侧出发、经开路径可达的原图顶点集 S。其边边界全由闭边组成：一条从 S 通向 S^c 的边不可能是开的，否则另一个端点就会落在 S 里。沿着 S 的边界从盒子顶端走到底端，边界边的对偶便构成一条闭对偶路径，把 n^ 的上下两边连起来。这就是 B^ 。（若 S 为空，则整个左侧都是闭的，对偶路径沿左边界走。） 高维中没有“单调耦合”可用，这条引理就是它在二维的替代品。d=2 中一切精确结果都从这里开始。

entries.heading: 4.2 为何自对偶点是 $1/2$
entries.text: 命题 4.3（★）。 对 {Z}^2 上 p=1/2 的键渗流，对每个 n 都有 证明。 引理 4.2 给出 对每个 p 成立。在 p 1-p 与颜色交换之下，B^ 变成开上下横穿；由正方形的四重对称性与 p=1/2 处的颜色对称性， 故 2 {P} {1/2}(A)=1。 这是一个值得注意的恒等式：无论尺寸多大，p=1/2 处的横穿概率都恰好是一半，而不只是近似一半。它是二维程序的一项锐利有限尺度检验；data/benchmarks.json 中的基准测试套件把它用作采样器的首要验证。 命题 4.3 没有 给出的是 p c=1/2。它只说明 p=1/2 是对偶变换的不动点，并没有说它就是临界点。原则上，一个模型可以在别处发生一阶相变，同时仍满足这个恒等式。弥合这道缺口，靠的是 Harris–Kesten 定理。

entries.heading: 4.3 Harris–Kesten：证明的架构
entries.text: 定理 4.4（Harris 1960；Kesten 1980）。 对 {Z}^2 上的键渗流，p c=1/2。 证明分两半，用到的工具不同。 下半部分，p c 1/2（Harris）。 假设 (1/2) 0。那么以正概率存在无穷开团簇，而由唯一性定理（定理 5.3，其成立不依赖于 p c 的值），它几乎必然唯一。唯一性加上正密度的一个标准推论是： n 存在开左右横穿的概率当 n 时趋于 1。无穷团簇具有正密度，因而会与大盒子的两侧都相交；横穿事件失败，只可能是团簇在盒子内部断开，而这一事件的概率按指数衰减。这与命题 4.3 矛盾——后者把每个 n 的概率都固定为 1/2。因此 (1/2)=0，p c 1/2。 从唯一性走到“横穿概率趋于一”这一步，是唯一非初等的成分；Grimmett 的 Percolation 第 8 章证明了它，可均性假设也正是在这里进入。下半部分其余的一切，都只是命题 4.3。 上半部分，p c 1/2（Kesten）。 发动机是 RSW 不等式。 定理 4.5（Russo 1978；Seymour–Welsh 1978）。 存在常数 0，使得对所有 p 与所有 n， 证明是粗粒化论证：把 2n n 的矩形分成四个 n n 的正方形；若长矩形被横穿，则或者有两个相邻正方形沿同一方向被横穿，或者存在互补方向上的对偶横穿；FKG 把这一择一情形转化为单个正方形的下界，再迭代该不等式，便把 改进为与 n 无关的常数。 有了 RSW，Kesten 的论证就是一个区块构造。取 p=1/2+ 。当 n 比 1/ 大得多时，给定的 n n 区块被左右横穿的概率至少为 ，而由 FKG，水平相邻区块的横穿会互相加强。沿宽度为 N 的矩形把这样一串区块粘接起来，便以随 N/n 指数趋于 1 的概率得到整个矩形的左右横穿。把这些矩形叠起来，再用“梯子”论证，就能对每个尺度给出到达距离 2^k 的开路径，其概率有常数下界；接着 Borel–Cantelli 论证给出 (1/2+ ) 0。于是对每个 0 都有 p c 1/2+ 。 注 4.6。 这个证明已被反复简化。Bollobás 与 Riordan（2006）的路线使用 Friedgut–Kalai 锐阈值定理；它在概念上更干净，但依赖另一个重量级结果。没有哪个证明是短的。对本图册而言，要紧的是结构：对偶给出不动点，RSW 给出不动点处的刚性，而刚性把不动点升级为临界点。

entries.heading: 4.4 匹配对、星–三角变换与更正后的三次方程
entries.anchor: 44-匹配对星三角变换与更正后的三次方程
entries.text: 定理 4.7（匹配关系）。 设 G,G^ 是一对匹配的周期平面图，且二者都是可均的。则 证明思路。 G 的一个构型与 G^ 上经颜色交换的对偶构型，在引理 4.2 的意义下互补。平面分离论证把有限盒子的命题提升到无穷情形：G 没有无穷开团簇，当且仅当 G^ 有无穷闭 -团簇。把“密度为 1-p 的闭 -团簇”翻译成“密度为 q 的开团簇”，便得到该恒等式。可均性假设用来排除一种可能：两侧都以正概率不发生渗流。 对于（三角格子 T，蜂窝格子 H）这一对，匹配关系给出一个方程。第二个方程是星–三角恒等式，代数正是在这里必须小心处理。 定理 4.8（Sykes–Essam 1964；★ 代数）。 对键渗流， 推导。 在三角格子的临界点 p=p c(T) 上工作，令 q=1-p 为闭键密度；由匹配关系，它也是蜂窝格子的临界密度。 一个星（一个顶点经三条键连到三个外围顶点）在键概率为 q 时，当且仅当三条键全开，才把三个外围顶点两两相连，这一事件的概率是 q^3。一个三角形在键概率为 p 时，只要三条键中至少两条为开，它的三个顶点便两两相连，这一事件的概率为 星–三角变换在临界点处把这两个三端网络等同起来，于是 代入 q=1-p，得 三次方程有三个实根：2 (10^ )、2 (50^ ) 与 -2 (70^ )；只有第一个落在 (0,1) 内，故 数值核验：取 p=0.34729635533386066，得 q^3=0.2780661432813856 与 3p^2-2p^3=0.2780661432813855，在双精度的最后一位上一致。 为何一个看似合理的捷径会失败。 一条诱人但错误的路线，把三角形的连通性与星的 密度 等同起来：3p^2-2p^3=1-p。这并不是星的三端连通性；星只有在三条键全开时才连接三个外围顶点，其概率是 (1-p)^3。错误的等式给出三次方程 它有根 p=1/2，另有两个根落在 (0,1) 之外。于是它“预测”键阈值为 1/2，而这个值实际上是三角格子的 位点 阈值。两者的数值差别很大（0.3473 对 0.5），而这两个数又常常被列在同一张表里，正因如此，出处才要紧。正确的三次方程给出 2 10^ ，与 Sykes 和 Essam（1964）一致。 注 4.9（Y–Δ 这一步的地位）。 恒等式 q^3=3p^2-2p^3 并不是单个星与单个三角形在分布意义下的等式：两个网络的圈结构不同，三个边界顶点的连通性分布也不同。它是随机簇模型 Yang–Baxter（星–三角）关系在 q { {RC}} 1 时的极限，用在三端连通函数的层面上；这里的 q { {RC}} 是随机簇的团簇权重，不是上文所用的闭键密度 q。把它当作可以逐三角形施加的局部恒等式，是常见的错误，只会得到无意义的结果；它是临界点上的恒等式，而它对键问题的严格论证，正是 Sykes–Essam 匹配论证的内容，后来由 Wierman 严格化。

entries.heading: 4.5 三角格子的位点阈值
entries.text: 定理 4.10。 三角格子上的位点渗流，p c=1/2。 论证（★ 结构）。 三角格子是全三角剖分的，每个面都是三角形；位点问题的匹配图是蜂窝格子，只是顶点与面的角色互换。此时星–三角变换作用于 位点 ：三角格子的一个位点连同它的六个邻居，对偶于蜂窝格子的一个六边形，六边形的六个位点正是这些邻居的对偶。密度为 p 时，一个位点开着的概率，等于对应六边形“被阻塞”的概率；全三角剖分的结构使这两个事件互补。因此 而该变换的自对偶点是 p=1/2。严格版本归功于 Wierman（1981）；完整叙述见 Grimmett（1999）§11.9。 Menshikov 与 Aizenman–Barsky 证明的是相变的锐性，而不是这个阈值的数值；二手叙述常把两组结果混为一谈。 推论 4.11。 若平面图 G 以三角格子为子图，则 p c^{ {site}}(G) 1/2，因为增加边与顶点不可能提高阈值。对任意平面图，并不存在这种形式的普适下界：在三角格子上加边会降低阈值，而含有三角子格的平面图可以低于 1/2。

entries.heading: 4.7 不应从中推出的东西
entries.text: 这张表容易引出一个错误的模式：配位数越大，阈值越低。这个模式平均而言是真的，但在定量上毫无用处。Kagome 格子的 z=4，位点阈值为 0.6527；正方格子的 z=4 与之相同，位点阈值却是 0.5927。差别来自环的结构，而不是度。p c 2/z 一类的公式，或者 Galam–Mauger 插值，在某些格子上能把表复现到几个百分点以内，在另一些格子上则错得离谱。它们不是定理，绝不应该用来“预测”一个真正要紧的阈值。第 11 章列出由此而来的测量陷阱。

entries.heading: 锐性与唯一性
entries.text: 两个定理把 p c 的定义变成一套可用的理论。第一个说，在 p c 以下，连通性按指数衰减；于是“不存在无限团簇”是关于每一个长度尺度的强命题，而不只是关于无穷远。第二个说，在 p c 以上恰好有一个无限团簇；于是“发生渗流”是整个系统的性质，而不是某个碰巧的团簇的性质。两个定理在 {Z}^d 上成立，也在所引结果覆盖的传递可均图上成立；它们的证明用的是完全不同的想法。
